In what follows, please find the results of additional analyses: variance inflation factors, the originally preregistered model, results without covariates, results with all participants (hence, including those removed due to speeding or response patterns), and frequentist robustness and moderation analyses. For the main analyses, see [Analyses](05a_analyses.html).

All analyses on this page focus on communication (the number of words), the main outcome of the study. Self-disclosure is only analyzed in the main analyses, because it is addressed in one additional research question (RQ2).

# Variance Inflation Factors

In what follows, you can find estimations of variance inflation factors, which help gauge multicollinearity. Generally, values above 5 or even 10 are considered problematic. However, these are only rules of thumb, and multicollinearity can occur with lower values. Indeed, although the values reported below are not above 5, they are increased, suggesting that multicollinearity might be at play here, which the preregistered analyses also confirm.

Each variable is regressed on all other privacy calculus variables (controlling for gender, age, and education). The VIF is then computed from the explained variance: VIF = 1 / (1 − R²). As in the preregistered analyses, trust is measured as specific trust here.

*Self-efficacy* regressed on the other variables:

```{r vif-self-eff}
model <- "
pri_con =~ PC01_01 + PC01_02 + PC01_04 + PC01_05 + PC01_06 + PC01_07 
grats_gen =~ GR02_01 + GR02_02 + GR02_03 + GR02_04 + GR02_05
pri_delib =~ PD01_01 + PD01_02 + PD01_03 + PD01_04 + PD01_05
self_eff =~ SE01_01 + SE01_02 + SE01_03 + SE01_04
SE01_01 ~~ a*SE01_02
SE01_03 ~~ a*SE01_04
trust_community =~ TR01_01 + TR01_02 + TR01_03
trust_provider =~ TR01_04 + TR01_05 + TR01_06 + TR01_07 + TR01_08 + TR01_09
trust_spec =~ trust_community + trust_provider

self_eff ~ pri_con + grats_gen + pri_delib + trust_spec

# Covariates
GR02_01 + GR02_02 + GR02_03 + GR02_04 + GR02_05 + PC01_01 + PC01_02 + PC01_04 + PC01_05 + PC01_06 + PC01_07 + TR01_01 + TR01_02 + TR01_03 + TR01_04 + TR01_05 + TR01_06 + TR01_07 + TR01_08 + TR01_09 + PD01_01 + PD01_02 + PD01_03 + PD01_04 + PD01_05 + SE01_01 + SE01_02 + SE01_03 + SE01_04 ~ male + age + edu
"
fit <- sem(model, data = d, estimator = "MLR", missing = "ML")
r_self_eff <- inspect(fit, what = "rsquare")["self_eff"] # extract rsquare
vif_self_eff <- 1 / (1 - r_self_eff) # compute vif
```

*Privacy deliberation* regressed on the other variables:

```{r vif-pri-delib}
model <- "
pri_con =~ PC01_01 + PC01_02 + PC01_04 + PC01_05 + PC01_06 + PC01_07 
grats_gen =~ GR02_01 + GR02_02 + GR02_03 + GR02_04 + GR02_05
pri_delib =~ PD01_01 + PD01_02 + PD01_03 + PD01_04 + PD01_05
self_eff =~ SE01_01 + SE01_02 + SE01_03 + SE01_04
SE01_01 ~~ a*SE01_02
SE01_03 ~~ a*SE01_04
trust_community =~ TR01_01 + TR01_02 + TR01_03
trust_provider =~ TR01_04 + TR01_05 + TR01_06 + TR01_07 + TR01_08 + TR01_09
trust_spec =~ trust_community + trust_provider
pri_delib ~ self_eff + pri_con + grats_gen + trust_spec

# Covariates
GR02_01 + GR02_02 + GR02_03 + GR02_04 + GR02_05 + PC01_01 + PC01_02 + PC01_04 + PC01_05 + PC01_06 + PC01_07 + TR01_01 + TR01_02 + TR01_03 + TR01_04 + TR01_05 + TR01_06 + TR01_07 + TR01_08 + TR01_09 + PD01_01 + PD01_02 + PD01_03 + PD01_04 + PD01_05 + SE01_01 + SE01_02 + SE01_03 + SE01_04 ~ male + age + edu
"
fit <- sem(model, data = d, estimator = "MLR", missing = "ML")
r_pri_delib <- inspect(fit, what = "rsquare")["pri_delib"]

```

# Originally Preregistered Model

We first analyze the model as it was initially preregistered. In the original preregistration, the outcome was communication including reactions: the number of words plus twice the number of likes and dislikes given, log-transformed (see [Open Science and Preregistration](appendix_prereg_note.qmd)). Trust was modeled as one factor combining general and specific trust.

```{r}
model <- "
pri_con =~ PC01_01 + PC01_02 + PC01_04 + PC01_05 + PC01_06 + PC01_07 
grats_gen =~ GR02_01 + GR02_02 + GR02_03 + GR02_04 + GR02_05
pri_delib =~ PD01_01 + PD01_02 + PD01_03 + PD01_04 + PD01_05
self_eff =~ SE01_01 + SE01_02 + SE01_03 + SE01_04
  SE01_01 ~~ x*SE01_02
  SE01_03 ~~ x*SE01_04
trust_community =~ TR02_01 + TR01_01 + TR01_02 + TR01_03
trust_provider =~ TR02_02 + TR01_04 + TR01_05 + TR01_06
trust_system =~ TR02_03 + TR01_07 + TR01_08 + TR01_09
trust =~ trust_community + trust_provider + trust_system

words_react_log ~ a1*pri_con + b1*grats_gen + c1*pri_delib + d1*self_eff + e1*trust

# Covariates
words_react_log + GR02_01 + GR02_02 + GR02_03 + GR02_04 + GR02_05 + PC01_01 + PC01_02 + PC01_04 + PC01_05 + PC01_06 + PC01_07 + TR02_01 + TR02_02 + TR02_03 + TR01_01 + TR01_02 + TR01_03 + TR01_04 + TR01_05 + TR01_06 + TR01_07 + TR01_08 + TR01_09 + PD01_01 + PD01_02 + PD01_03 + PD01_04 + PD01_05 + SE01_01 + SE01_02 + SE01_03 + SE01_04 ~ male + age + edu
"
fit_prereg <- sem(model, data = d, estimator = "MLR", missing = "ML")
summary(fit_prereg, fit = TRUE, std = TRUE)
rsquare_fit_prereg <- inspect(fit_prereg, what = "rsquare")["words_react_log"]
```

Model fit is not optimal but still acceptable, `r td::fit_txt(fit_prereg)`. The results show the same problems of multicollinearity, namely that trust reduces online communication (despite a positive and more plausible bivariate relation).

# Results Without Covariates

As stated in our preregistration, we also provide the results without controlling for covariates. Note that we are now using the updated preregistered model as reported in the paper.

```{r}
model <- "
  pri_con =~ PC01_01 + PC01_02 + PC01_04 + PC01_05 + PC01_06 + PC01_07 
  grats_gen =~ GR02_01 + GR02_02 + GR02_03 + GR02_04 + GR02_05
  pri_delib =~ PD01_01 + PD01_02 + PD01_03 + PD01_04 + PD01_05
  self_eff =~ SE01_01 + SE01_02 + SE01_03 + SE01_04
  SE01_01 ~~ x*SE01_02
  SE01_03 ~~ x*SE01_04
  trust_community =~ TR01_01 + TR01_02 + TR01_03
  trust_provider =~ TR01_04 + TR01_05 + TR01_06
  trust_system =~ TR01_07 + TR01_08 + TR01_09
  trust_spec =~ trust_community + trust_provider + trust_system

words_log ~ a1*pri_con + b1*grats_gen + c1*pri_delib + d1*self_eff + e1*trust_spec
"
fit_prereg <- sem(model, data = d, estimator = "MLR", missing = "ML")
summary(fit_prereg, fit = TRUE, std = TRUE)
rsquare_fit_prereg <- inspect(fit_prereg, what = "rsquare")["words_log"]
```

The results remain virtually the same (see [Analyses](05a_analyses.html)).

# Results Including Removed Participants

As stated in the preregistration, we also report the analyses including the deleted participants.

We first need to rerun the baseline model to get new factor scores (output not shown here).

```{r results='hide'}
model_baseline <- "
  pri_con =~ PC01_01 + PC01_02 + PC01_04 + PC01_05 + PC01_06 + PC01_07
  grats_gen =~ GR02_01 + GR02_02 + GR02_03 + GR02_04 + GR02_05
  grats_inf =~ GR01_01 + GR01_02 + GR01_03 
  grats_rel =~ GR01_04 + GR01_05 + GR01_06 
  grats_par =~ GR01_07 + GR01_08 + GR01_09
  grats_ide =~ GR01_10 + GR01_11 + GR01_12 
  grats_ext =~ GR01_13 + GR01_14 + GR01_15
  grats_spec =~ grats_inf + grats_rel + grats_par + grats_ide + grats_ext
  pri_delib =~ PD01_01 + PD01_02 + PD01_03 + PD01_04 + PD01_05
  trust_gen =~ TR02_01 + TR02_02 + TR02_03
  trust_community =~ TR01_01 + TR01_02 + TR01_03
  trust_provider =~ TR01_04 + TR01_05 + TR01_06
  trust_system =~ TR01_07 + TR01_08 + TR01_09
  trust_spec =~ trust_community + trust_provider + trust_system
  self_eff =~ SE01_01 + SE01_02 + SE01_03 + SE01_04
    SE01_01 ~~ x*SE01_02
    SE01_03 ~~ x*SE01_04
  Words_log =~ words_log
  
  Words_log ~~ a1*pri_con + b1*grats_gen + c1*pri_delib + d1*self_eff + e1*trust_spec + f1*trust_gen + g1*grats_spec
"
fit_baseline <- sem(model_baseline, data = d_all, missing = "ML")
summary(fit_baseline, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE)
```

```{r results='hide'}
# extract model predicted values for items & calc means
d_fs <- lavPredict(fit_baseline, type = "ov") %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  mutate(version = d_all$version, 
         grats_gen_fs = rowMeans(select(., starts_with("GR02"))),
         grats_spec_fs = rowMeans(select(., starts_with("GR01"))), 
         pri_con_fs = rowMeans(select(., starts_with("PC01"))),
         trust_gen_fs = rowMeans(select(., TR02_01, TR02_02, TR02_03)),
         trust_spec_fs = rowMeans(select(., TR01_01: TR01_09)),
         pri_del_fs = rowMeans(select(., starts_with("PD01"))),
         self_eff_fs = rowMeans(select(., starts_with("SE01")))) %>%
  select(version, pri_con_fs, grats_gen_fs, grats_spec_fs, pri_del_fs, self_eff_fs, trust_gen_fs, trust_spec_fs, words_log)

# combine d with d factor scores
d_all %<>% cbind(select(d_fs, -version, -words_log))
```

Let's now inspect the results of the (updated) preregistered model including removed cases.

```{r}
model <- "
  pri_con =~ PC01_01 + PC01_02 + PC01_04 + PC01_05 + PC01_06 + PC01_07 
  grats_gen =~ GR02_01 + GR02_02 + GR02_03 + GR02_04 + GR02_05
  pri_delib =~ PD01_01 + PD01_02 + PD01_03 + PD01_04 + PD01_05
  self_eff =~ SE01_01 + SE01_02 + SE01_03 + SE01_04
  SE01_01 ~~ x*SE01_02
  SE01_03 ~~ x*SE01_04
  trust_community =~ TR01_01 + TR01_02 + TR01_03
  trust_provider =~ TR01_04 + TR01_05 + TR01_06
  trust_system =~ TR01_07 + TR01_08 + TR01_09
  trust_spec =~ trust_community + trust_provider + trust_system

words_log ~ a1*pri_con + b1*grats_gen + c1*pri_delib + d1*self_eff + e1*trust_spec

# Covariates
words_log + GR02_01 + GR02_02 + GR02_03 + GR02_04 + GR02_05 + PC01_01 + PC01_02 + PC01_04 + PC01_05 + PC01_06 + PC01_07 + TR01_01 + TR01_02 + TR01_03 + TR01_04 + TR01_05 + TR01_06 + TR01_07 + TR01_08 + TR01_09 + PD01_01 + PD01_02 + PD01_03 + PD01_04 + PD01_05 + SE01_01 + SE01_02 + SE01_03 + SE01_04 ~ male + age + edu

# Covariances
male ~~ age + edu
age ~~ edu
"
fit_prereg <- sem(model, data = d_all, estimator = "MLR", missing = "ML")
summary(fit_prereg, fit = TRUE, std = TRUE)
```

The analyses now include the data of `r nrow(d_all)` participants. When comparing the analyses, the results do not differ in any meaningful way.

# Frequentist Robustness and Moderation Analyses

In what follows, we report frequentist robustness checks of the main analyses (see [Analyses](05a_analyses.html)). These models are easier to interpret than the Bayesian hurdle models. As in the paper, the main focus is on communication.

We estimate three types of models:

1. **Logistic regressions:** Did participants communicate at all?
2. **OLS regressions** with the log-transformed number of words: How much did participants communicate?
3. **Negative binomial regressions** with the raw number of words: How much did participants communicate? These models account for the count nature and the skewness of the data.

For each predictor, we also test whether its effect depends on the popularity cues (moderation). The first model of each type includes the predictor and the experimental condition, the second model adds their interaction, and the third model additionally controls for gender, age, and education. All privacy calculus variables are mean scores on the original 1–7 scale (not standardized). They use the same items as in the main analyses, including general trust.

As an additional check, we analyze a second outcome: communication including reactions (the number of words plus twice the number of likes and dislikes given). This was the outcome of the original preregistration. Note that it is *not* the self-disclosure index of the main analyses.

## Setup

The following models are fast. We therefore turn off caching and code reformatting.

```{r}
#| label: options-frequentist
#| cache: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(cache = FALSE, tidy = FALSE)
```

Load the packages. The package `conflicted` makes sure that functions with the same name in different packages (e.g., `select()` in dplyr and MASS) are not mixed up.

```{r}
#| label: load-packages-frequentist

options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org"))

packages <- c("tidyverse", "texreg", "marginaleffects", "ggpubr", "MASS", "DescTools", "conflicted")

# install missing packages, then load all
load_p <- function(){
  for (p in packages) {
    if (!requireNamespace(p, quietly = TRUE)) {
      install.packages(p)
    }
    library(p, character.only = TRUE)
  }
}

load_p()

# resolve conflicts between packages
conflict_scout()
conflicts_prefer(dplyr::select)
conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter)
```

Load the data, as saved at the end of the main analyses (final sample).

```{r}
#| label: read-data-frequentist
data <- readr::read_csv("data/data.csv")
```

Compute the privacy calculus variables as mean scores. We use the same items as in the main analyses (e.g., without the deleted items, and general trust).

```{r}
#| label: construct-means
data <- data |> 
  rowwise() |> 
  mutate(
    self_eff = mean(c_across(SE01_01:SE01_04), na.rm = TRUE),
    pri_con = mean(c_across(c(PC01_01, PC01_02, PC01_04:PC01_07)), na.rm = TRUE),
    grats_gen = mean(c_across(GR02_01:GR02_05), na.rm = TRUE),
    pri_delib = mean(c_across(PD01_01:PD01_05), na.rm = TRUE),
    # general trust in the provider, the website, and the other users (as in the main analyses)
    # note: the items are listed individually, because the TR02 items are not next to each other in the data
    trust_gen = mean(c(TR02_01, TR02_02, TR02_03), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |> 
  ungroup()
```

Compute the outcomes: whether participants communicated at all, and the second outcome (words + reactions).

```{r}
#| label: construct-outcomes
data <- data |> 
  mutate(
    # did participants communicate at all? (0 = no, 1 = yes)
    communicated = if_else(words > 0, 1, 0),
    # words + reactions: likes and dislikes given count twice
    words_react = words + 2 * reactions,
    words_react_log = log1p(words_react)
  )
```

## Whether Participants Communicated (Logistic Regressions)

We first analyze whether participants communicated at all. Each model includes one privacy calculus variable and the experimental condition.

```{r}
#| label: lr-models-communicated
commented_lr_1 <- glm(communicated ~ 
    self_eff + version,
    data = data,
    family = binomial(link = "logit")
    )

commented_lr_2 <- glm(communicated ~ 
    pri_con + version,
    data = data,
    family = binomial(link = "logit")
    )

commented_lr_3 <- glm(communicated ~ 
    grats_gen + version,
    data = data,
    family = binomial(link = "logit")
    )

commented_lr_4 <- glm(communicated ~ 
    pri_delib + version,
    data = data,
    family = binomial(link = "logit")
    )

commented_lr_5 <- glm(communicated ~ 
    trust_gen + version,
    data = data,
    family = binomial(link = "logit")
    )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-comm-lr
#| tbl-cap: "Effect of Privacy Calculus Variables on Decision to Communicate"
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
#| results: asis

htmlreg(
  list(commented_lr_1,
       commented_lr_2,
       commented_lr_3,
       commented_lr_4,
       commented_lr_5
       ),
  custom.model.names = c(
    "LR Model 1",
    "LR Model 2",
    "LR Model 3",
    "LR Model 4",
    "LR Model 5"
    ),
  custom.header = list(
  "DV: Communicated" = 1:5
  ),
  custom.coef.map = list(
    "self_eff" = "Self-Efficacy",
    "pri_con" = "Privacy Concerns",
    "grats_gen" = "Gratifications",
    "pri_delib" = "Privacy Deliberation",
    "trust_gen" = "Trust",
    "versionLike" = "Like Button",
    "versionLike & dislike" = "Like Dislike Buttons",
    "(Intercept)" = "Constant"
  ),
  custom.gof.rows = list(
    "Estimator" = c("Logit", "Logit", "Logit", "Logit", "Logit")
    ),
  digits = 2,
  single.row = FALSE,
  caption.above = TRUE,
  table = FALSE
)
```

All privacy calculus variables predicted whether participants communicated at all, in the expected direction: Participants with more self-efficacy, gratifications, and trust were more likely to communicate, and participants with more privacy concerns and privacy deliberation were less likely to communicate. The popularity cues did not affect whether participants communicated.

## Moderation: Do Popularity Cues Change the Effects on How Much Participants Communicated?

In this section, we test whether the effects of the privacy calculus variables on how much participants communicated depend on the popularity cues. The main result is a moderation of self-efficacy: Self-efficacy increased communication in all models, but with like buttons this effect was significantly weaker than in the control condition. The effects of privacy concerns, gratifications, privacy deliberation, and trust did not depend on the popularity cues.

For each privacy calculus variable, we estimate six models: three OLS regressions with the log-transformed number of words (first three models in each table) and three negative binomial regressions with the raw number of words (last three models). We then repeat these models with words + reactions as outcome.

### Self-Efficacy

Does self-efficacy predict how much participants wrote, and does this depend on the popularity cues? First, the OLS regressions with the log-transformed number of words.

```{r}
#| label: words-ols-self-eff
words_log_ols1_se <- glm(words_log ~ 
    self_eff + version,
    data = data,
    family = "gaussian"
    )

words_log_ols2_se <- glm(words_log ~ 
    self_eff * version,
    data = data,
    family = "gaussian"
    )

words_log_ols3_se <- glm(words_log ~ 
    self_eff * version + 
    male + 
    age + 
    edu_fac,
    data = data,
    family = "gaussian"
    )
```

Second, the negative binomial regressions with the raw number of words.

```{r}
#| label: words-nb-self-eff
words_nb1_se <- glm.nb(words ~ 
    self_eff + version,
    data = data
    )

words_nb2_se <- glm.nb(words ~ 
    self_eff * version,
    data = data
    )

words_nb3_se <- glm.nb(words ~ 
    self_eff * version + 
    male + 
    age + 
    edu_fac,
    data = data
    )
```

@tbl-words-self-eff shows the results.

```{r}

    "Model 2",
    "Model 3",
    "Model 4",
    "Model 5",
    "Model 6"
    ),
  custom.header = list(
  "DV: Words (log)" = 1:3, "DV: Words" = 4:6
  ),
  custom.coef.map = list(
    "self_eff" = "Self-Efficacy",
    "versionLike" = "Like Button",
    "versionLike & dislike" = "Like Dislike Buttons",
    "male" = "Male",
    "age" = "Age",
    "self_eff:versionLike" = "Self-Efficacy x Like",
    "self_eff:versionLike & dislike" = "Self-Efficacy x Like Dislike",

  single.row = FALSE,
  caption.above = TRUE,
  table = FALSE
)
```

Self-efficacy was significantly and positively related to communication in all six models. The interaction between self-efficacy and like buttons was significant and negative in all four models that include it (Models 2, 3, 5, and 6): With like buttons, the effect of self-efficacy was weaker than in the control condition. The interaction between self-efficacy and like & dislike buttons was not significant in any model. Note that in models with an interaction, the coefficient of the like button shows its effect for participants with a self-efficacy of 0, which lies outside the scale (1–7). It should therefore not be interpreted on its own. We illustrate the moderation below, after the models for words + reactions.

@fig-meplot shows the marginal effect of self-efficacy in each condition, for both outcomes (Models 3 and 9).

```{r}
#| label: fig-meplot
#| include: true
#| fig-cap: "Marginal Effects of Self-Efficacy on Communication"
#| fig-cap-location: bottom

# common theme for both plots
me_theme <- theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_line(
      linetype = "dashed",
      color = "gray80",
      linewidth = .2
    ),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x  = element_text(size = 8),
    axis.text.y  = element_text(size = 8),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 10, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 10, margin = margin(r = 15)),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

# plot A: marginal effect of self-efficacy per condition, outcome words (log)
marg_A <- plot_slopes(
  words_log_ols3_se,
  variables = "self_eff",
  condition = "version",
  conf_level = 0.95,
) +
  geom_rug(
    data = data,
    mapping = aes(x = version),
    sides = "b",
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    colour = "black",
    alpha = 0.6,
    size = 0.3,
    length = grid::unit(0.03, "npc")
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  me_theme +
  labs(
    x = "Affordance",
    y = "Marginal Effect of Self-Efficacy",
    caption = "Model 3 (words, log)"
  )

# plot B: same for words + reactions (log)
marg_B <- plot_slopes(
  words_react_log_ols3_se,
  variables = "self_eff",
  condition = "version",
  conf_level = 0.95
) +
  geom_rug(
    data = data,
    mapping = aes(x = version),
    sides = "b",
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    colour = "black",
    alpha = 0.6,
    size = 0.3,
    length = grid::unit(0.03, "npc")
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  me_theme +
  labs(
    x = "Affordance",
    y = "Marginal Effect of Self-Efficacy",
    caption = "Model 9 (words + reactions, log)"
  )

ggarrange(
  marg_A, marg_B,
  ncol = 2, nrow = 1,
  common.legend = TRUE,
  legend = "bottom"
)
```

In both models, the effect of self-efficacy is significant and positive in all three conditions (none of the confidence intervals includes zero). With like buttons, however, the effect is only about half as large as in the control condition. @fig-predplot shows the same pattern as predicted values: With increasing self-efficacy, the number of words increases more strongly in the control condition than with like buttons.

```{r}
#| label: fig-predplot
#| include: true
#| fig-cap: "Predicted Values for Words (log), Model 3"
#| fig-cap-location: bottom

# predict words (log) across self-efficacy, holding the controls constant
new_vals <- expand.grid(
  self_eff = seq(1, 7, by = 0.25),
  version = c("Control", "Like", "Like & dislike"),
  male = Mode(data$male, na.rm = T),
  age = mean(data$age, na.rm = T),
  edu_fac = Mode(data$edu_fac, na.rm = T)
)

pred <- new_vals |> 
  mutate(yhat = predict(words_log_ols3_se, new_vals))

pred |> 
  filter(version != "Like & dislike") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = self_eff, y = yhat, color = version)) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
  ) +
  labs(x = "Self-Efficacy", y = "Predicted Words (log)",
    color = "Affordance")
```

### All Predictors Combined

Finally, we include all privacy calculus variables in one model. Because the predictors are correlated, these models should be interpreted with caution (see [Variance Inflation Factors](#variance-inflation-factors)). The interaction is only tested for self-efficacy, the only variable with a significant interaction above.

Here, we only report OLS regressions. The negative binomial regressions with all predictors did not converge: the outcome contains many zeros and is strongly skewed (which is also why the main analyses use hurdle models).

```{r}
#| label: words-ols-all
words_log_ols1_comp <- glm(words_log ~ 
    self_eff + 
    version +
    pri_con + 
    grats_gen + 
    pri_delib +
    trust_gen,
    data = data,
    family = "gaussian"
    )

words_log_ols2_comp <- glm(words_log ~ 
    self_eff * version + 
    pri_con + 
    grats_gen + 
    pri_delib +
    trust_gen,
    data = data,
    family = "gaussian"
    )

words_log_ols3_comp <- glm(words_log ~ 
    self_eff * version + 
    pri_con + 
    grats_gen + 
    pri_delib +
    trust_gen +
    male + 
    age + 
    edu_fac,
    data = data,
    family = "gaussian"
    )
```

@tbl-words-all shows the results.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-words-all
#| tbl-cap: "Effect of Privacy Calculus on Communication Conditional on Affordances"
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom
#| results: asis

htmlreg(
  list(words_log_ols1_comp,
       words_log_ols2_comp,
       words_log_ols3_comp
       ),
  custom.model.names = c(
    "Model 61",
    "Model 62",
    "Model 63"
    ),
  custom.header = list(
  "DV: Words (log)" = 1:3
  ),
  custom.coef.map = list(
    "versionLike" = "Like Button",
    "versionLike & dislike" = "Like Dislike Buttons",
    "self_eff" = "Self-Efficacy",
    "pri_con" = "Privacy Concerns",
    "grats_gen" = "Gratifications",
    "pri_delib" = "Privacy Deliberation",
    "trust_gen" = "Trust",
    "male" = "Male",
    "age" = "Age",
    "self_eff:versionLike" = "Self-Efficacy x Like",
    "self_eff:versionLike & dislike" = "Self-Efficacy x Like Dislike",
    "(Intercept)" = "Constant"
  ),
  custom.gof.rows = list(
    "Estimator" = c("OLS", "OLS", "OLS"),
    "Controls (gender, age, education)" = c("No", "No", "Yes")
    ),
  digits = 2,
  single.row = FALSE,
  caption.above = TRUE,
  table = FALSE
)
```

When all variables are analyzed together, two variables remain significant in all three models (Models 61 to 63): self-efficacy (positive) and privacy deliberation (negative). Privacy concerns, gratifications, and trust are no longer significant, which is in line with the problems of multicollinearity described above. The interaction between self-efficacy and like buttons remains significant and negative (Models 62 and 63); the interaction with like & dislike buttons is not significant.
